lesson.title: Bytes All the Way Down: What "Text Mode" Really Means
lesson.summary: Every file on disk is ultimately just a sequence of bytes, and text mode versus binary mode is about whether Python translates those bytes into characters using an encoding, or hands them to you raw.
lesson.body:
Recall that at the lowest level, everything stored on a computer, including every file, is a sequence of bits grouped into bytes, each byte just a number from 0 to 255. A CSV file, a JSON file, a photograph, and a song are all, underneath, nothing more than a long run of these byte values sitting on disk. The difference between a "text file" and a "binary file" is not something stamped into the bytes themselves, since a byte does not know what it means. The difference is entirely about how a program chooses to interpret those bytes when it reads them, and Python makes you choose that interpretation explicitly through the mode you pass to open().

Every file you have opened so far in this course, including the CSV and JSON files from the last three chapters, used text mode, which is the default. In text mode, when you write a string with f.write(), Python encodes each character into one or more bytes according to a specific encoding, most commonly UTF-8 today, and writes those bytes to disk. When you read with f.read(), Python does the reverse, decoding the raw bytes back into a Python str using that same encoding. This is exactly why you have been passing encoding="utf-8" to open(): you are telling Python precisely which translation table to use in both directions, so that the bytes on disk and the characters in your program agree with each other.

Binary mode skips that translation completely. Adding a "b" to the mode string, as in "rb" for reading or "wb" for writing, tells Python not to encode or decode anything: you get back the file's raw bytes exactly as they sit on disk, as a Python bytes object instead of a str, and if you write, whatever bytes object you hand over is written unchanged. Binary mode is what you use for files that are not meant to be read as characters at all, images, audio clips, PDFs, compiled programs, because forcing those bytes through a text encoding would either fail outright or corrupt the data.

The clearest way to see the difference is to write one small text file and then read the same file back both ways.

```python
text = "caf\u00e9 \u2603"  # "café" plus a snowman character
with open("note.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(text)

with open("note.txt", "rb") as f:
    raw = f.read()
print(raw)

with open("note.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    back = f.read()
print(back)
print(text == back)
```

This prints:

```
b'caf\xc3\xa9 \xe2\x98\x83'
café ☃
True
```

The original text is 7 characters long (c, a, f, e-with-accent, space, snowman, and that is it), but the raw bytes printed in binary mode show 10 bytes: the plain ASCII characters c, a, f each take one byte, but the accented e takes two bytes (\xc3\xa9) and the snowman takes three bytes (\xe2\x98\x83) under UTF-8 encoding. This is the bits-and-bytes idea in action: a "character" is a concept your program works with, but on disk it is really some specific number of bytes, and the encoding is the agreed-upon rule for translating between the two. Read in text mode, Python quietly redoes that translation for you and you get the readable string back; read in binary mode, you see the raw bytes with no translation at all.

The practical rule going forward is simple: if the file holds human-readable text, structured data, CSV, JSON, or plain notes, open it in text mode with an explicit encoding, exactly as you have been doing. If the file holds anything else, images, audio, or other data not meant to be read as characters, open it in binary mode instead.
